tables.heading: Supplied help
rows: “In the beginning”: a supplied temporal use of **on**, with dative **anginne**.
“Created,” third-person singular preterite. In the opening, the subject **God** follows the verb; word order alone does not identify the object.
“Heaven”: accusative **singular** of weak feminine **heofone**, a variant of the masculine **heofon** learned above. It is not masculine **heofon**'s plural.
Connective “now/for its part”; “empty and void.” The two adjectives are predicate feminine nominative singular with **eorðe**.
“Over the surface of the deep.” **Ofer** here governs dative **brādnesse**, the head. **Ðǣre nēowolnesse** is its genitive dependent; **ðǣre** belongs to that dependent.

“Was borne/carried over the waters,” contextually “moved over the waters.” **Wæs gefęred** is a passive phrase; **gefęred** is a past participle. Here **ofer** has accusative plural **wæteru**, unlike the preceding dative construction.
“Then said”: **cwæð** is third-person singular preterite; this **ðā** is the adverb “then,” not the article.
“Let light come to be.” **Geweorðe** is a finite third-person singular present subjunctive (also called optative), expressing a wish or command.
“Light was made/came into being.” **Wearð** is a third-person singular preterite used here with past participle **geworht** in a passive phrase.

“Then saw that it was good.” **Geseah** is third-person singular preterite; **ðā** is “then”; **ðæt** is the conjunction “that.” **Hit**, “it,” refers to neuter **lēoht**; **gōd** is a neuter nominative singular predicate adjective. The copula stands at the end of the embedded clause.
“He separated”: **hē** is nominative singular, referring to God; **gedǣlde** is third-person singular preterite. The object and **fram** phrase use §9.
**hēt ðæt lēoht Dæg, and ðā ðīestru Niht**

“[He] called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” **Hēt** is third-person singular preterite, with God/he understood as subject. **Ðæt lēoht** and **ðā ðīestru** are accusative objects; **Dæg** and **Niht** are accusative names applied to them. Here **ðæt** and **ðā** are articles.
**Ðā wæs geworden ǣfen and morgen ān dæg.**

“Then there came to be evening and morning: one day.” **Wæs geworden** expresses a resulting state or completed coming-to-be, “had come to be”; **geworden** is a past participle. **Ān dæg** is “one day,” not the ordinal “first day.” Treat this closing formula as a whole.

let them separate; let them shine; let them illuminate. Supplied plural present optatives with the lights as subject.
for signs / seasons / days / years. Tō governs these datives in a supplied function or purpose construction.

for the illumination of … ; dative līehtinge contains a dependent genitive day or night.
he set/placed; supplied past form of the prefixed verb. Its subject continues God/hē, although no subject is repeated in this clause. Hīe is the accusative object “them”.
so that they might shine … . Here ðæt introduces purpose. Preserve the short i in past optative scinen, contrasting present scīnen earlier.
over the earth. The whole phrase is supplied. Eorðan can be accusative or dative singular in this spelling; no unique choice is required.
might rule over; might separate. Supplied plural past optatives continuing the purpose clause. Gīemden governs the following genitives.
then saw that … ; supplied strong past verb and content clause. Here ðæt is a conjunction, not an article.
